entries.definition: To make something impossible, especially in advance; to rule out by necessity.
entries.plain: To make something impossible before it can happen.
entries.etymology: Latin praecludere, from prae- (before) + claudere (to shut).
entries.exampleClinical: Her renal function precludes contrast imaging, so we'll settle for a non-contrast study.
entries.exampleCasual: A student budget kind of precludes spontaneous weekend trips.
entries.usageNote: Formal. A thing precludes another thing; a person is precluded FROM doing something — never 'preclude to do'.

entries.definition: To remove a difficulty or need so that it no longer has to be dealt with.
entries.plain: To make a problem or need unnecessary.
entries.etymology: Latin obviare 'to meet in the way', from ob- (against) + via (way).
entries.exampleClinical: Catching the diagnosis early might obviate the need for surgery altogether.
entries.exampleCasual: A shared calendar obviates roughly ninety percent of our 'who forgot to tell whom' arguments.
entries.usageNote: Most often in 'obviate the need for'. Subtly different from 'prevent': you remove the necessity, not the event.

entries.definition: To confirm or give support to a statement, theory, or finding with additional evidence.
entries.plain: To back up a claim with more evidence.
entries.etymology: Latin corroborare 'to strengthen', from cor- (intensive) + robur (strength).
entries.exampleClinical: The collateral history from his wife corroborated the timeline he was too confused to give us himself.
entries.exampleCasual: Two other people corroborated her version, so the argument quietly ended.
entries.usageNote: Evidence corroborates a claim. Stronger and more formal than 'support'; pairs naturally with 'independently'.

entries.definition: To provide evidence to support or prove the truth of a claim.
entries.plain: To prove a claim with solid evidence.
entries.etymology: Latin substantia 'substance' — to give substance to.
entries.exampleClinical: The biopsy substantiated what the scan had only hinted at.
entries.exampleCasual: He made big promises about the project but never substantiated a single one.
entries.usageNote: The negative 'unsubstantiated' (claims, rumors) is extremely common. Close to 'corroborate' but emphasizes proving, not just supporting.

entries.definition: To reduce the force, effect, or value of something; to make weaker or thinner.
entries.plain: To weaken or lessen something.
entries.etymology: Latin attenuare 'to make thin', from ad- (to) + tenuis (thin).
entries.exampleClinical: The vaccine uses an attenuated strain — weakened just enough to teach the immune system without causing disease.
entries.exampleCasual: Distance attenuates most friendships unless you actually put the work in.
entries.usageNote: Common in science (attenuated virus, attenuated signal) and argument. Opposite of 'amplify'. More precise than plain 'reduce'.

entries.definition: To make a bad or unsatisfactory situation better.
entries.plain: To improve a bad situation.
entries.etymology: Latin melior 'better', via French améliorer.
entries.exampleClinical: Simple measures — elevation, analgesia, reassurance — ameliorated the swelling within a day.
entries.exampleCasual: A good night's sleep does more to ameliorate my mood than any amount of advice.
entries.usageNote: Formal cousin of 'improve', usually applied to situations and conditions rather than objects. Opposite: 'aggravate'.

entries.definition: To emphasize or call special attention to something.
entries.plain: To stress how important something is.
entries.etymology: From 'under' + 'score' (a line), originally a line drawn beneath text.
entries.exampleClinical: The case underscores how an atypical presentation can hide a textbook diagnosis.
entries.exampleCasual: Her promotion underscored just how much quiet work she'd been doing all year.
entries.usageNote: Often introduces a lesson: 'this case underscores the need for...'. Interchangeable with 'underline' in this figurative sense.

entries.definition: To put forward an idea as a basis for argument or discussion; to assume as true.
entries.plain: To propose an idea as a starting point.
entries.etymology: Latin ponere 'to place', past participle positus.
entries.exampleClinical: The authors posit an autoimmune mechanism, though they're careful to call it a hypothesis.
entries.exampleCasual: Let me posit, just for the sake of argument, that we're both a little bit wrong.
entries.usageNote: Academic register. Often 'posit that...'. Implies a proposal to be tested, not a settled fact.

entries.definition: To admit, often reluctantly, that something is true or valid; to yield a point.
entries.plain: To admit something is true, even if you'd rather not.
entries.etymology: Latin concedere 'to yield', from con- (with) + cedere (to go, give way).
entries.exampleClinical: I'd concede that the evidence here is thin, but the risk of missing it is too high to ignore.
entries.exampleCasual: He finally conceded that I'd been right about the shortcut all along.
entries.usageNote: Useful for balanced argument: concede a minor point to win the major one. 'Grant' is a softer synonym.

entries.definition: To describe or mark out precisely; to indicate the exact boundaries of something.
entries.plain: To map out or describe something clearly and exactly.
entries.etymology: Latin delineare 'to sketch out', from de- + linea (line).
entries.exampleClinical: The MRI delineated the tumor margins far better than the ultrasound could.
entries.exampleCasual: We sat down and delineated exactly who was responsible for what before the trip.
entries.usageNote: Two senses: to describe in detail, and to mark physical boundaries. 'Clearly delineated' is the stock collocation.

entries.definition: To make something clear by explaining it; to throw light on.
entries.plain: To explain something so it becomes clear.
entries.etymology: Latin elucidare 'to make clear', from e- (out) + lucidus (bright).
collocations: further studies are needed to elucidate
entries.exampleClinical: Further studies are needed to elucidate exactly how the drug protects the kidney.
entries.exampleCasual: Could you elucidate that last point? I followed you right up until the diagram.
entries.usageNote: Shares the 'luc' (light) root with 'lucid'. Academic favorite, especially '...needed to elucidate the mechanism'.

entries.definition: To extend known information to estimate or infer something beyond the available data.
entries.plain: To predict the unknown by extending what you already know.
entries.etymology: From 'extra-' (outside) + a back-formation from 'interpolate'.
entries.exampleClinical: These results come from young adults, so it's risky to extrapolate them to frail elderly patients.
entries.exampleCasual: Don't extrapolate from one bad date to the entire concept of romance.
entries.usageNote: Takes 'from' (the data) and 'to' (the new case). Often carries a warning: over-extrapolation is a classic reasoning error.

entries.definition: To reach a conclusion from evidence and reasoning rather than from explicit statements.
entries.plain: To work something out from the clues.
entries.etymology: Latin inferre 'to bring in', from in- + ferre (to carry).
entries.exampleClinical: From the pattern of weakness we inferred a peripheral cause rather than a central one.
entries.exampleCasual: From his silence I inferred that the news wasn't good.
entries.usageNote: The listener infers; the speaker implies. Confusing the two is one of English's most common upper-level errors — see the Mix-ups tab.

entries.definition: To suggest something as a logical consequence or hint without stating it directly.
entries.plain: To hint at something without saying it outright.
entries.etymology: Latin implicare 'to enfold', from in- + plicare (to fold).
entries.exampleClinical: A normal D-dimer doesn't prove anything is fine, but in a low-risk patient it implies that a clot is unlikely.
entries.exampleCasual: I'm not saying you were wrong — I'm just implying it very loudly.
entries.usageNote: The mirror of 'infer': speakers and evidence imply; listeners infer. Keep the direction straight and you'll sound precise.

entries.definition: To go without or give up something one might have had, especially by choice.
entries.plain: To choose to do without something.
entries.etymology: Old English forgan 'to go without', from for- (away) + gan (to go).
entries.exampleClinical: After a long talk, the family chose to forgo further chemotherapy in favor of comfort.
entries.exampleCasual: I forwent dessert tonight, a decision I'm already regretting.
entries.usageNote: Past tense 'forwent', participle 'forgone' (as in 'a foregone conclusion'). Don't confuse with 'forego' meaning 'to precede'.

entries.definition: To prevent something by taking action ahead of time; to head off.
entries.plain: To stop something by acting before it happens.
entries.etymology: Old English foresteall 'an ambush', literally a standing in the way beforehand.
entries.exampleClinical: She addressed every likely worry up front to forestall the family's questions before they arose.
entries.exampleCasual: He raised his hand to forestall the inevitable 'but actually' from across the table.
entries.usageNote: Implies anticipating and neutralizing. Close to 'pre-empt'; both carry the sense of acting just in time.

entries.definition: To take the place of something previous, especially something now outdated.
entries.plain: To replace something older or outdated.
entries.etymology: Latin supersedere 'to sit above, refrain from', from super- + sedere (to sit).
entries.exampleClinical: The new guideline supersedes the 2019 version, so the old thresholds no longer apply.
entries.exampleCasual: Streaming pretty much superseded the DVD shelf in my house overnight.
entries.usageNote: Note the spelling: -sede, not -cede (the only English word with this ending). Often passive: 'has been superseded by'.

entries.definition: To make something less severe, serious, or painful.
entries.plain: To soften the impact of something bad.
entries.etymology: Latin mitigare 'to soften', from mitis (mild) + agere (to drive).
entries.exampleClinical: Early mobilization mitigates the risk of clots without any added cost.
entries.exampleCasual: Booking the early train mitigated at least some of the chaos of moving day.
entries.usageNote: Don't confuse with 'militate' (to weigh against, as in 'factors militate against surgery'). 'Mitigating factors' is a fixed legal-ish phrase.

entries.definition: To examine something closely and critically.
entries.plain: To look at something very carefully and critically.
entries.etymology: Latin scrutari 'to search, examine', originally 'to sort rubbish' (scruta).
entries.exampleClinical: We scrutinized the old notes line by line and found the allergy everyone had missed.
entries.exampleCasual: He scrutinized the menu like it was a final exam.
entries.usageNote: Noun: scrutiny. Implies critical, suspicious attention, not just looking. 'Under scrutiny' = being closely watched.

entries.definition: To perceive or recognize something, especially something not immediately obvious; to distinguish.
entries.plain: To make something out, or tell two things apart.
entries.etymology: Latin discernere 'to separate', from dis- (apart) + cernere (to sift).
entries.exampleClinical: It was hard to discern, on the grainy film, whether the line was a fracture or just an artifact.
entries.exampleCasual: I couldn't quite discern whether she was joking or genuinely annoyed.
entries.usageNote: Adjective 'discerning' means having good judgment ('a discerning reader'). Slightly formal; implies effort or subtlety.

entries.definition: To suppose that something is true without certain evidence; to guess from partial information.
entries.plain: To guess based on limited clues.
entries.etymology: Old French surmise 'accusation', from Latin supermittere (to put upon).
entries.exampleClinical: From the empty pill bottles by the bed we could only surmise what had happened overnight.
entries.exampleCasual: From the silence on the other end, I surmised the news wasn't going to be fun.
entries.usageNote: Also a noun: 'that's pure surmise'. More tentative than 'conclude'; signals a reasoned guess, not a fact.

entries.definition: To make two apparently conflicting things compatible; also, to restore friendly relations.
entries.plain: To make two things that seem to clash fit together.
entries.etymology: Latin reconciliare 'to bring together again', from re- + conciliare (to unite).
entries.exampleClinical: I couldn't reconcile the normal scan with how sick she clearly was, so I kept digging.
entries.exampleCasual: It's hard to reconcile his easygoing texts with how tense he seemed in person.
entries.usageNote: 'Reconcile A with B'. In medicine, 'medication reconciliation' is checking the list matches reality — a near-technical sense.

entries.definition: To shock or excite someone into taking sudden, decisive action.
entries.plain: To jolt people into action.
entries.etymology: From Luigi Galvani, who made frog legs twitch with electricity.
entries.exampleClinical: The near-miss galvanized the whole department into rewriting the handover protocol.
entries.exampleCasual: Nothing galvanizes a group project like a deadline twelve hours away.
entries.usageNote: Often 'galvanize [someone] into action'. The electrical metaphor is alive: a sudden, energizing jolt.

entries.definition: To refer to something indirectly or in passing.
entries.plain: To mention something without naming it directly.
entries.etymology: Latin alludere 'to play with', from ad- (to) + ludere (to play).
entries.exampleClinical: He alluded to past mental-health struggles but clearly wasn't ready to give details.
entries.exampleCasual: She alluded to some big news but refused to actually say what it was.
entries.usageNote: Always 'allude TO'. Noun: allusion (an indirect reference). Don't confuse with 'elude' (to escape) — see Mix-ups.

entries.definition: To provide clear evidence of something, or to declare it to be true.
entries.plain: To show or swear that something is true.
entries.etymology: Latin attestari 'to bear witness', from ad- + testis (witness).
entries.exampleClinical: The thickness of the chart attests to how long this illness has been part of his life.
entries.exampleCasual: As anyone who's lived with me can attest, I am hopeless before coffee.
entries.usageNote: Usually 'attest TO something'. Slightly formal. Things can attest (give evidence) as well as people.

entries.definition: To require something as a prior condition; to assume it in advance.
entries.plain: To take something for granted as a starting assumption.
entries.etymology: Latin prae- (before) + supponere (to put under, assume).
entries.exampleClinical: That treatment plan presupposes she can afford the medication, which we hadn't actually checked.
entries.exampleCasual: Your question presupposes I had any plan at all, which is generous of you.
entries.usageNote: Highlights a hidden assumption baked into a claim. A favorite in critical thinking and philosophy of argument.

entries.definition: Most noticeable or important; standing out from the rest.
entries.plain: The most important and noticeable point.
entries.etymology: Latin salire 'to leap' — a salient point 'leaps out'.
entries.exampleClinical: Strip away the noise and the salient feature is the weight loss — that's what reframes everything.
entries.exampleCasual: The salient detail she left out was that the apartment had no windows.
entries.usageNote: 'Salient point' and 'salient features' are the go-to collocations. From 'leap' — the idea jumps out at you.

entries.definition: Of an argument or case, clear, logical, and convincing.
entries.plain: Clear and convincing, in the way a good argument is.
entries.etymology: Latin cogere 'to drive together, compel', from co- + agere (to drive).
entries.exampleClinical: She made a cogent case for discharge, and the consultant signed off without a single objection.
entries.exampleCasual: Give me one cogent reason to wake up at five for a 'sunrise hike' and I'll consider it.
entries.usageNote: Describes reasoning, not facts: a cogent argument. Adverb 'cogently'. A notch more formal than 'convincing'.

entries.definition: Able to be defended or maintained against objection or attack.
entries.plain: A position you can reasonably defend.
entries.etymology: Latin tenere 'to hold', via French tenable.
entries.exampleClinical: Once the cultures came back, the original diagnosis was simply no longer tenable.
entries.exampleCasual: His 'I'll start the diet Monday' position has not been tenable for several years now.
entries.usageNote: The negative 'untenable' is more common in practice ('an untenable situation'). From 'hold' — a position you can hold onto.

entries.definition: Very economical, sometimes to the point of stinginess; in science, using the fewest assumptions.
entries.plain: Spare and economical — using as little as possible.
entries.etymology: Latin parsimonia 'thrift', from parcere (to spare).
entries.exampleClinical: One diagnosis that explains all three findings is the more parsimonious story, and usually the right one.
entries.exampleCasual: He's famously parsimonious with compliments, so 'not bad' from him is basically a standing ovation.
entries.usageNote: In science, 'the most parsimonious explanation' echoes Occam's razor. In everyday use it can mean stingy — context decides the tone.

entries.definition: Showing great, careful attention to detail.
entries.plain: Extremely careful and precise about details.
entries.etymology: Latin meticulosus 'fearful', from metus (fear) — fear of getting it wrong.
entries.exampleClinical: Her notes were so meticulous that the night team could reconstruct the entire day from them.
entries.exampleCasual: He's meticulous about his coffee — bean weight, water temperature, the lot.
entries.usageNote: Strongly positive. Adverb 'meticulously' often pairs with documented, planned, recorded. The fear-based etymology is a nice memory hook.

entries.definition: Hasty and not thorough; done quickly with little attention to detail.
entries.plain: Quick and shallow, not thorough.
entries.etymology: Latin cursorius 'of running', from currere (to run).
entries.exampleClinical: A cursory look at the chart missed it; the diagnosis was hiding in a labs tab nobody opened.
entries.exampleCasual: I gave the terms and conditions my usual cursory glance and clicked accept.
entries.usageNote: From 'run' — done at a run. 'A cursory glance/examination' are the stock phrases. Mildly critical in tone.

entries.definition: Done merely as a duty, without real interest, care, or enthusiasm.
entries.plain: Done half-heartedly, just to get it over with.
entries.etymology: Latin perfunctus 'having performed', from perfungi (to discharge a duty).
entries.exampleClinical: A perfunctory neuro exam ticks the box but misses the subtle drift that actually matters.
entries.exampleCasual: He gave a perfunctory 'sorry' that fooled absolutely no one.
entries.usageNote: Implies going through the motions. Close to 'cursory', but emphasizes lack of sincerity rather than lack of time.

entries.definition: Understood or implied without being stated outright.
entries.plain: Understood without being said.
entries.etymology: Latin tacitus 'silent', from tacere (to be silent).
entries.exampleClinical: There was a tacit understanding on the team that the sickest patient got seen first, no discussion needed.
entries.exampleCasual: We had a tacit agreement never to mention the karaoke incident again.
entries.usageNote: From 'silent'. Pairs with agreement, approval, understanding. Opposite of 'explicit'; close to 'implicit'.

entries.definition: Apparently or as stated, but perhaps not actually so.
entries.plain: Supposedly — on the surface, but maybe not really.
entries.etymology: Latin ostendere 'to show', from ob- + tendere (to stretch).
entries.exampleClinical: He came in ostensibly for a sick note, but the real reason surfaced twenty minutes into the visit.
entries.exampleCasual: She dropped by ostensibly to return a book, and stayed four hours.
entries.usageNote: Signals a gap between the stated reason and the likely real one. A subtle, useful skeptic's adverb.

entries.definition: Based on observation, experiment, or experience rather than theory alone.
entries.plain: Based on real-world evidence, not just theory.
entries.etymology: Greek empeirikos 'experienced', from peira (trial).
entries.exampleClinical: It's a tidy theory, but there's surprisingly little empirical evidence behind it.
entries.exampleCasual: My claim that the corner café is best is, I admit, not exactly empirical.
entries.usageNote: Contrast with 'anecdotal' (single stories) and 'theoretical'. In clinical use, 'empiric' (a variant) means treating before test results.

entries.definition: Based on personal accounts or isolated examples rather than systematic evidence.
entries.plain: Based on individual stories, not solid data.
entries.etymology: Greek anekdota 'things unpublished', from an- (not) + ekdotos (given out).
entries.exampleClinical: The benefit is still anecdotal — a few striking cases, but no trial has put it to the test.
entries.exampleCasual: My evidence that black cats are friendlier is entirely anecdotal and entirely sincere.
entries.usageNote: Often slightly dismissive: 'that's just anecdotal'. The phrase 'the plural of anecdote is not data' captures the warning.

entries.definition: Strongly influential in shaping later developments; foundational.
entries.plain: A work so influential that everything later grows from it.
entries.etymology: Latin seminalis 'of seed', from semen (seed).
entries.exampleClinical: That seminal 1980s trial is still the reason we treat this the way we do.
entries.exampleCasual: Her debut album was seminal — you can hear its fingerprints all over the genre now.
entries.usageNote: From 'seed' — ideas that later work grows from. 'A seminal paper/work' is the stock phrase in academic writing.

entries.definition: Very weak or slight; lacking a sound basis.
entries.plain: Thin and shaky — barely holding together.
entries.etymology: Latin tenuis 'thin'.
entries.exampleClinical: The connection between the rash and the new drug was tenuous, but worth flagging just in case.
entries.exampleCasual: My grasp of the plot was tenuous from about episode three onward.
entries.usageNote: Figurative: a tenuous link, argument, or grip. From 'thin'. Stronger and more elegant than 'weak'.

entries.definition: Dangerously unstable or insecure; likely to collapse or fail.
entries.plain: Shaky and likely to fall apart at any moment.
entries.etymology: Latin precarius 'obtained by prayer, uncertain', from prex (prayer).
entries.exampleClinical: His blood pressure was precarious all night — propped up by drips that nobody dared turn down.
entries.exampleCasual: The whole pile of books was balanced precariously on the arm of the sofa.
entries.usageNote: Adverb 'precariously' often pairs with 'balanced' or 'perched'. The prayer-based root hints at 'depending on chance'.

entries.definition: Extremely complex and difficult to follow.
entries.plain: So twisted and complicated it's hard to follow.
entries.etymology: Latin convolvere 'to roll together', from con- + volvere (to roll).
entries.exampleClinical: His insurance situation was so convoluted that arranging the scan took longer than reading it.
entries.exampleCasual: She told a wonderfully convoluted story that somehow ended back where it started.
entries.usageNote: Usually critical: needlessly complicated. Literally 'rolled together'. 'Intricate' can be admiring; 'convoluted' rarely is.

entries.definition: Clear and easy to understand; also, mentally clear and able to think clearly.
entries.plain: Clear-minded, or clearly expressed.
entries.etymology: Latin lucidus 'bright, clear', from lux (light).
entries.exampleClinical: Between bouts of confusion she had a lucid interval long enough to tell us what she actually wanted.
entries.exampleCasual: After the third coffee I finally felt lucid enough to tackle the spreadsheet.
entries.usageNote: 'A lucid interval' is a near-clinical phrase (a clear window in confusion). Shares the 'light' root with 'elucidate'.

entries.definition: Having or showing sharp, accurate judgment and insight.
entries.plain: Sharp and quick to understand what's really going on.
entries.etymology: Latin astutus 'crafty', from astus (cunning).
entries.exampleClinical: It was an astute call by the junior — she spotted the subtle asymmetry everyone else walked past.
entries.exampleCasual: That was an astute read of the room; you knew to change the subject before I did.
entries.usageNote: Strongly positive: praises sharp judgment. 'Clinically astute' is high praise for a colleague. Close to 'shrewd' but cleaner in tone.

entries.definition: Honest and straightforward, especially about something difficult.
entries.plain: Openly honest, even when it's awkward.
entries.etymology: Latin candidus 'white, pure', from candere (to shine).
entries.exampleClinical: I'll be candid: the odds aren't good, but they aren't zero either.
entries.exampleCasual: In a rare candid moment, he admitted the whole plan had been improvised.
entries.usageNote: Noun: candor. 'To be candid' works like 'to be honest' as a softener before bad news. Warmer than 'blunt'.

entries.definition: Skilled at saying or doing the right thing without causing offence.
entries.plain: Careful and sensitive about other people's feelings.
entries.etymology: Latin tactus 'touch' — a fine sense of touch in handling people.
collocations: a tactful way of putting it
entries.exampleClinical: She found a tactful way to raise the drinking without putting him on the defensive.
entries.exampleCasual: There's a tactful way to tell a friend their haircut is bold, and I did not find it.
entries.usageNote: Noun: tact. Pairs naturally with 'but honest' — the art of being kind and truthful at once.

entries.definition: Able to recover quickly from difficulty; able to spring back into shape.
entries.plain: Quick to bounce back from hard times.
entries.etymology: Latin resilire 'to leap back', from re- + salire (to jump).
entries.exampleClinical: Kids are astonishingly resilient — she was running around the ward two days after the operation.
entries.exampleCasual: My houseplants are weirdly resilient; I neglect them and they thrive out of spite.
entries.usageNote: Noun: resilience, a buzzword in both medicine and self-help. The 'leap back' root makes the meaning easy to remember.

entries.definition: Seeming difficult or intimidating enough to discourage someone.
entries.plain: So big or hard it's intimidating.
entries.etymology: Old French danter 'to tame', from Latin domitare.
entries.exampleClinical: The reading list for the rotation looked daunting until I broke it into a page a day.
entries.exampleCasual: Moving to a new city alone is daunting, but it's the good kind of scary.
entries.usageNote: 'A daunting task/prospect' are the natural collocations. The verb 'undaunted' (not discouraged) is a useful spin-off.

entries.definition: So small or unimportant as to be not worth considering.
entries.plain: Too small to matter.
entries.etymology: Latin neglegere 'to disregard', from neg- (not) + legere (to gather, pick).
entries.exampleClinical: The extra radiation from one chest film is negligible compared to the risk of missing the pneumonia.
entries.exampleCasual: The price difference was negligible, so I just bought the nicer one.
entries.usageNote: Means small enough to ignore. Don't confuse with 'negligent' (carelessly failing a duty) — same root, opposite tone.

entries.definition: Of considerable importance, size, or worth.
entries.plain: Large or significant.
entries.etymology: Latin substantia 'substance' — having real substance.
entries.exampleClinical: There was a substantial improvement after the second dose — not subtle, you could see it across the room.
entries.exampleCasual: She made a substantial dent in the reading over the weekend.
entries.usageNote: Quantity and importance both. Adverb 'substantially' ('substantially higher') is common in formal writing. Opposite: 'negligible'.

entries.definition: Severe and bare in appearance; or, of a contrast or difference, sharply evident.
entries.plain: Harsh and bare, or sharply obvious.
entries.etymology: Old English stearc 'stiff, strong'.
entries.exampleClinical: The before-and-after scans showed a stark contrast that needed no commentary.
entries.exampleCasual: There's a stark difference between his weekday and weekend personalities.
entries.usageNote: 'A stark contrast/difference' is the dominant collocation. Also means bleak ('stark landscape') or blunt ('the stark truth').

entries.definition: Clearly visible or attracting notice and attention.
entries.plain: Standing out so much you can't miss it.
entries.etymology: Latin conspicuus 'visible', from conspicere (to look at).
entries.exampleClinical: The one conspicuous thing about his otherwise normal exam was how anxious he seemed.
entries.exampleCasual: His silence at the meeting was conspicuous; usually he can't be stopped.
entries.usageNote: 'Conspicuous by its absence' is a fixed ironic phrase — something noticeable precisely because it's missing.

entries.definition: Difficult to find, catch, achieve, or pin down.
entries.plain: Hard to catch, find, or define.
entries.etymology: Latin eludere 'to escape', from e- (out) + ludere (to play).
entries.exampleClinical: The unifying diagnosis stayed elusive for a week, hiding behind three unrelated-looking complaints.
entries.exampleCasual: A good night's sleep has been frustratingly elusive since the newborn arrived.
entries.usageNote: From the same root as 'elude'. 'Remains elusive' is the academic stock phrase for an unsolved problem.

entries.definition: A subtle difference or shade of meaning, feeling, or expression.
entries.plain: A small, subtle difference that changes the meaning.
entries.etymology: French nuance 'shade of color', from nue (cloud).
entries.exampleClinical: The skill is hearing the nuance: 'a bit of pain' from a stoic patient can mean agony.
entries.exampleCasual: A lot of the nuance of her texts is carried entirely by where she puts the full stops.
entries.usageNote: Adjective 'nuanced' (a nuanced argument) is high praise. Non-native speakers often flatten nuance — naming it helps you hear it.

entries.definition: A warning or qualification that limits or clarifies a statement.
entries.plain: A 'but be careful' note attached to a claim.
entries.etymology: Latin caveat 'let him beware', from cavere (to beware).
entries.exampleClinical: The drug works well, with the caveat that you have to monitor the kidneys closely.
entries.exampleCasual: I'll lend you the car, with one caveat: you fill the tank.
entries.usageNote: 'With the caveat that...' is the workhorse phrase. Still literally Latin ('let him beware'); singular, plural 'caveats'.

entries.definition: A confusing and difficult problem or question.
entries.plain: A puzzling, hard-to-solve problem.
entries.etymology: Origin uncertain; a 17th-century mock-Latin coinage.
entries.exampleClinical: The mismatch between her symptoms and every test result was a genuine diagnostic conundrum.
entries.exampleCasual: Whether to text back immediately or play it cool is the eternal conundrum.
entries.usageNote: 'A diagnostic conundrum' is a beloved medical phrase for a baffling case. Slightly playful in tone compared with 'dilemma'.

entries.definition: A difficult, unpleasant, or embarrassing situation that is hard to get out of.
entries.plain: A tricky, awkward situation with no easy way out.
entries.etymology: Latin praedicamentum 'something asserted', later 'a category, situation'.
entries.exampleClinical: Refusing the operation while clearly needing it left everyone in an ethical predicament.
entries.exampleCasual: I'd double-booked myself, which is a predicament entirely of my own making.
entries.usageNote: Emphasizes a tough situation; 'quandary' leans more toward mental indecision. 'In a predicament' is the usual frame.

entries.definition: A difference or inconsistency between things that should match.
entries.plain: A mismatch between two things that ought to agree.
entries.etymology: Latin discrepare 'to sound differently', from dis- + crepare (to rattle).
entries.exampleClinical: There was a discrepancy between his reported dose and what the pharmacy had dispensed.
entries.exampleCasual: The discrepancy between the photos and the actual apartment was, let's say, creative.
entries.usageNote: 'A discrepancy between A and B'. More precise than 'difference': it implies things that were supposed to match but don't.

entries.definition: A great or unfair difference between things or groups.
entries.plain: A big, often unfair gap between things.
entries.etymology: Latin dis- (not) + paritas (equality), from par (equal).
entries.exampleClinical: The talk was on health disparities — why outcomes differ so sharply between neighborhoods barely a mile apart.
entries.exampleCasual: There's quite a disparity between how hard he says he works and how hard he works.
entries.usageNote: Often carries a sense of unfairness, unlike the neutral 'discrepancy'. 'Health disparities' is a major public-health term.

entries.definition: A close, harmonious relationship with mutual understanding and easy communication.
entries.plain: A good, easy connection with someone.
entries.etymology: French rapporter 'to bring back', from re- + apporter (to bring).
entries.exampleClinical: Two minutes of genuine small talk built more rapport than any checklist could.
entries.exampleCasual: We had an instant rapport — by the end of the coffee it felt like we'd known each other for years.
entries.usageNote: Note the silent 't': rap-POR. 'Build/establish rapport' is core to clinical and interview skills. No plural in normal use.

entries.definition: Outward behavior, manner, and bearing toward others.
entries.plain: The way someone carries and conducts themselves.
entries.etymology: Old French demener 'to conduct', from de- + mener (to lead).
entries.exampleClinical: His calm demeanor slipped only once, when we mentioned his daughter — and that told us a lot.
entries.exampleCasual: She has a relaxed demeanor that somehow makes everyone around her relax too.
entries.usageNote: British spelling 'demeanour'. Describes the visible manner, not inner feeling. 'A change in demeanor' is a useful observational phrase.

entries.definition: Calm self-control, especially under pressure.
entries.plain: Staying calm and steady under stress.
entries.etymology: From 'compose' (to settle, arrange) + -ure.
entries.exampleClinical: Even as the rhythm collapsed, she kept her composure and ran the algorithm step by step.
entries.exampleCasual: I lost my composure completely when the waiter brought out the surprise cake.
entries.usageNote: 'Keep/regain/lose composure' are the set phrases. A key professional quality; 'equanimity' is its more literary cousin.

entries.definition: A natural tendency or inclination to behave in a particular way.
entries.plain: A built-in tendency to do something.
entries.etymology: Latin propensus 'inclined', from pro- + pendere (to hang).
entries.exampleClinical: The condition carries a propensity for clotting, so prophylaxis isn't optional here.
entries.exampleCasual: He has a propensity for starting projects he never quite finishes.
entries.usageNote: Takes 'for' (a noun) or 'to' (a verb): propensity for risk, propensity to overthink. Formal cousin of 'tendency'.

entries.definition: A complex or unwelcome consequence of an action or decision.
entries.plain: A knock-on effect, usually complicated or unwanted.
entries.etymology: Latin ramus 'branch' — consequences branching out.
entries.exampleClinical: Labeling someone with that diagnosis has ramifications for insurance, employment, and self-image — not just treatment.
entries.exampleCasual: I hadn't thought through the ramifications of adopting two kittens at once.
entries.usageNote: Usually plural and often negative. The 'branch' root captures how one decision splinters into many effects.

entries.definition: A natural consequence or result that follows logically from something already proven or stated.
entries.plain: Something that naturally follows from what's already true.
entries.etymology: Latin corollarium 'a gift, deduction', from corolla (small garland).
entries.exampleClinical: The corollary of an aging population is a steady rise in chronic disease — one follows from the other.
entries.exampleCasual: The corollary of saying yes to everything is having time for nothing.
entries.usageNote: More logical than 'ramification': a corollary follows by reasoning, not by side effect. Common in maths and formal argument.

entries.definition: Though; even if. Used to introduce a concession in a compact way.
entries.plain: Though — a tidy way to add a 'but'.
entries.etymology: Contraction of 'all be it' — 'although it be'.
entries.exampleClinical: He responded to treatment, albeit more slowly than we'd hoped.
entries.exampleCasual: She agreed to come, albeit with a great deal of dramatic sighing.
entries.usageNote: Introduces a short concession, usually mid-sentence and followed by a phrase, not a full clause: 'albeit slowly', not 'albeit it was slow'.

entries.definition: In spite of; without being prevented by.
entries.plain: Despite.
entries.etymology: From 'not' + 'withstanding' (resisting) — not being resisted by.
entries.exampleClinical: Notwithstanding the normal labs, the clinical picture was alarming enough to admit him.
entries.exampleCasual: Notwithstanding the rain, the whole thing went ahead as planned.
entries.usageNote: Can go before or after its noun: 'notwithstanding the cost' or 'the cost notwithstanding'. Formal; a heavyweight 'despite'.

entries.definition: In contrast or comparison with the fact that; used to set two things against each other.
entries.plain: While by contrast.
entries.etymology: From 'where' + 'as'.
entries.exampleClinical: The first drug acts within minutes, whereas the second can take weeks to reach full effect.
entries.exampleCasual: I love an early start, whereas my flatmate considers anything before noon a personal attack.
entries.usageNote: Joins two contrasting clauses. More formal than 'while' and unambiguous (no time meaning). Common in academic comparison.

entries.definition: By that means; as a result of that action.
entries.plain: And in that way / as a result.
entries.etymology: From 'there' + 'by'.
entries.exampleClinical: We treated the cause rather than the symptom, thereby avoiding a cabinet full of unnecessary pills.
entries.exampleCasual: She batch-cooks on Sundays, thereby reclaiming about five weeknight hours.
entries.usageNote: Followed by an -ing clause: 'thereby reducing risk'. A compact, formal way to link an action to its outcome.

entries.definition: Until now or until the point in time under discussion.
entries.plain: Up to now.
entries.etymology: From 'hither' (to here) + 'to'.
entries.exampleClinical: The scan revealed a hitherto unsuspected mass, found entirely by accident.
entries.exampleCasual: The trip opened up a hitherto unimagined love of mountain villages.
entries.usageNote: Formal and slightly literary. Often 'hitherto + past participle' ('hitherto unknown'). Its forward-looking partner is 'henceforth'.

entries.definition: Introducing a statement that reverses or contrasts with the previous one.
entries.plain: The other way around.
entries.etymology: Latin conversus 'turned around', from convertere (to turn about).
entries.exampleClinical: Too little fluid harms the kidneys; conversely, too much floods the lungs — the art is the middle.
entries.exampleCasual: I work best late at night; conversely, my brother is useless after about nine.
entries.usageNote: Signals a logical reversal, often a symmetrical opposite. Stronger and more precise than 'on the other hand'.

entries.definition: To the extent that; only to the degree that something is true.
entries.plain: To the extent that.
entries.etymology: From 'in so far as' — within that distance or degree.
entries.exampleClinical: The treatment helps, insofar as it controls symptoms — it doesn't touch the underlying cause.
entries.exampleCasual: I'm a morning person, insofar as I'm technically awake and upright before nine.
entries.usageNote: Adds a precise limit to a claim. Formal and a little academic; signals careful, qualified reasoning.

entries.definition: Used to introduce a qualification or contrast to what you have just said.
entries.plain: Even so / but still.
entries.etymology: Elliptical for 'that having been said'.
entries.exampleClinical: The prognosis is serious. That said, people in her situation do sometimes surprise us.
entries.exampleCasual: The film dragged a bit. That said, the ending genuinely got me.
entries.usageNote: Conversational pivot that concedes a point then softens it. 'Having said that' and 'that being said' are equivalents.

entries.definition: The general meaning or main point of something, without the details.
entries.plain: The main point, in a nutshell.
entries.etymology: Old French gist 'it lies', from Latin jacere — 'where the essence lies'.
entries.exampleClinical: I didn't catch every word of the German paper, but I got the gist from the figures.
entries.exampleCasual: Just give me the gist — I don't need the full play-by-play.
entries.usageNote: Usually 'get the gist' or 'the gist of'. Informal but extremely common. 'Drift' ('catch my drift') is a close cousin.

entries.definition: A special skill or talent for doing something, often acquired with practice.
entries.plain: A natural skill or trick for doing something well.
entries.etymology: Middle English knak 'a sharp blow, trick'.
entries.exampleClinical: She has a knack for calming agitated patients that you simply can't teach from a textbook.
entries.exampleCasual: There's a knack to flipping an omelette; I have not yet acquired it.
entries.usageNote: 'A knack for [noun/-ing]' or 'the knack of'. Informal and warm. Implies an almost intuitive skill.

entries.definition: A feeling or guess based on intuition rather than evidence.
entries.plain: A gut feeling.
entries.etymology: From 'hunch' (to push) — originally a nudge or hint.
entries.exampleClinical: On a hunch I rechecked the glucose, and that hunch turned out to be the whole diagnosis.
entries.exampleCasual: I had a hunch you'd be running late, so I brought a book.
entries.usageNote: 'On a hunch' and 'a hunch that...' are the natural frames. Informal but respected — experienced clinicians trust theirs.

entries.definition: Something good that happens by chance rather than skill or planning.
entries.plain: A lucky accident.
entries.etymology: 19th-century billiards slang for a lucky shot.
entries.exampleClinical: Finding the tumour that early was honestly a fluke — the scan was for something else entirely.
entries.exampleCasual: My one good golf shot was a total fluke and I have never repeated it.
entries.usageNote: Implies luck, not skill. 'No fluke' insists something was earned. Informal; often self-deprecating.

entries.definition: A reversal or check in progress; something that delays or undoes advancement.
entries.plain: A step backward that slows your progress.
entries.etymology: From the phrasal verb 'set back' (to delay).
entries.exampleClinical: The infection was a setback, but a course of antibiotics put recovery back on track.
entries.exampleCasual: Losing the draft was a setback, though rewriting it actually made it better.
entries.usageNote: 'Suffer/hit a setback'. Implies temporary, recoverable difficulty — not total failure. Common in recovery and project talk.

entries.definition: Freedom or room to act, vary, or make decisions within limits.
entries.plain: Room to maneuver.
entries.etymology: Nautical: the sideways drift of a ship from its course.
entries.exampleClinical: The protocol gives you some leeway on timing, so use judgment rather than the clock.
entries.exampleCasual: My boss gives me a lot of leeway on how I structure my day, which I appreciate.
entries.usageNote: Uncountable: 'some leeway', 'a bit of leeway'. Nautical origin (sideways drift). Close to 'latitude' in the figurative sense.

entries.definition: To estimate or judge a quantity, level, or reaction; to assess.
entries.plain: To size up or estimate something.
entries.etymology: Old North French gauger 'to measure'.
entries.exampleClinical: I asked an open question first, just to gauge how much she already understood about the diagnosis.
entries.exampleCasual: I sent a casual text to gauge whether he was still annoyed.
entries.usageNote: Tricky spelling: g-a-u-g-e, but said 'gage'. 'Hard to gauge' is a common frame for uncertain estimates.

entries.definition: To define, identify, or establish something precisely; or to get a firm commitment from someone.
entries.plain: To nail something down exactly.
entries.etymology: From physically pinning something so it can't move.
entries.exampleClinical: The trigger was hard to pin down — the reaction never showed up the same way twice.
entries.exampleCasual: He's impossible to pin down to an actual date; everything is 'sometime soon'.
entries.usageNote: Two senses: pin down a fact (identify precisely) and pin down a person (extract a commitment). 'Hard to pin down' is very common.

entries.definition: To quickly improve or refresh a skill or knowledge you already have but have neglected.
entries.plain: To refresh a rusty skill.
entries.etymology: From 'brush up' — to clean and restore by brushing.
entries.exampleClinical: I brushed up on my ECG reading the night before the cardiology rotation started.
entries.exampleCasual: I really should brush up on my French before the trip.
entries.usageNote: Always 'brush up ON something'. Implies refreshing existing-but-rusty knowledge, not learning from scratch.

entries.definition: To think about something carefully and at length before deciding.
entries.plain: To turn something over in your mind.
entries.etymology: From 'mull' (to grind, ponder), origin uncertain.
entries.exampleClinical: I gave them the options and the weekend to mull it over before deciding.
entries.exampleCasual: Let me mull it over and I'll text you tomorrow.
entries.usageNote: 'Mull it over' is the everyday frame for taking time to decide. Warm and unhurried in tone; informal.

entries.definition: To make brief contact with someone to share updates or check in.
entries.plain: To check in briefly with someone.
entries.etymology: From baseball — touching a base to stay safe.
entries.exampleClinical: I'll touch base with the consultant before we commit to discharging her.
entries.exampleCasual: Let's touch base next week once things calm down.
entries.usageNote: Business and ward favorite. 'Touch base WITH someone'. Slightly corporate but ubiquitous; means a short check-in, not a full meeting.

entries.definition: The quality of being open, honest, and direct in expression.
entries.plain: Straightforward honesty.
entries.etymology: Latin candor 'whiteness, sincerity', from candere (to shine).
entries.exampleClinical: She spoke about her prognosis with a candor that caught the whole team off guard.
entries.exampleCasual: I appreciated his candor — he told me the haircut was a mistake before anyone else would.
entries.usageNote: British spelling 'candour'. The noun behind 'candid'. 'Disarming candor' is a lovely set phrase.

entries.definition: Careful, persistent effort and conscientiousness in work or duty.
entries.plain: Steady, careful hard work.
entries.etymology: Latin diligentia 'attentiveness', from diligere (to value, take care).
entries.exampleClinical: It was sheer diligence — rechecking every result — that caught the labeling error before it caused harm.
entries.exampleCasual: She applied to grad schools with a diligence the rest of us could only admire.
entries.usageNote: 'Due diligence' is a fixed phrase for proper investigation before a decision. Adjective: diligent. Strongly positive.

entries.definition: A tendency or susceptibility to a condition, behavior, or attitude, present in advance.
entries.plain: A built-in tendency toward something, often before it appears.
entries.etymology: Latin prae- (before) + disponere (to arrange).
entries.exampleClinical: A family history like that suggests a genetic predisposition rather than bad luck.
entries.exampleCasual: He has a predisposition to assume the worst, which makes him a terrible person to text vaguely.
entries.usageNote: Bridges medical ('genetic predisposition') and everyday ('a predisposition to optimism'). Takes 'to'. Verb: predispose.

entries.definition: Having sharp practical judgment, especially about people or situations.
entries.plain: Cleverly practical and hard to fool.
entries.etymology: Middle English shrewe 'a wicked person' — sense softened over time.
entries.exampleClinical: It was a shrewd move to admit her overnight rather than trust a reassuring single set of numbers.
entries.exampleCasual: She's a shrewd negotiator — somehow we ended up paying her to take the sofa.
entries.usageNote: Practical cleverness, especially about people and money. Slightly more street-smart in flavor than 'astute'.

entries.definition: Very detailed and complicated in a way that can be admirable.
entries.plain: Detailed and complex, often impressively so.
entries.etymology: Latin intricare 'to entangle', from in- + tricae (perplexities).
entries.exampleClinical: The intricate interplay of hormones here is genuinely beautiful once it finally clicks.
entries.exampleCasual: The cake had the most intricate icing I've ever been afraid to cut into.
entries.usageNote: Often admiring, unlike the critical 'convoluted'. 'Intricately linked/woven' are common. Praises complexity that works.

entries.definition: Very great or intense; or showing deep insight and understanding.
entries.plain: Very deep — in effect or in insight.
entries.etymology: Latin profundus 'deep', from pro- + fundus (bottom).
entries.exampleClinical: The anemia was profound — a hemoglobin that low explained every bit of her exhaustion.
entries.exampleCasual: She made one profound comment and then went straight back to talking about snacks.
entries.usageNote: Two senses: intense in degree ('profound hypotension') and deep in thought ('a profound observation'). Context separates them.

entries.definition: So delicate or precise as to be difficult to notice or describe.
entries.plain: Fine and hard to notice.
entries.etymology: Latin subtilis 'fine, delicate', literally 'finely woven'.
entries.exampleClinical: The signs were subtle — a slight drift of one arm, a faint slurring — but together they spelled a stroke.
entries.exampleCasual: He dropped a subtle hint about his birthday that was approximately as subtle as a brass band.
entries.usageNote: Silent 'b': SUT-uhl. Noun: subtlety. 'Subtle signs' is a clinical favorite for findings that are easy to miss.

entries.definition: Speaking plainly and directly, sometimes without regard for others' feelings.
entries.plain: Direct and plain-spoken, sometimes too much so.
entries.etymology: Middle English 'dull, not sharp', later applied to speech.
collocations: blunt to the point of rudeness
entries.exampleClinical: To be blunt, the surgery is risky — but doing nothing is riskier.
entries.exampleCasual: She's refreshingly blunt; you never have to decode what she actually means.
entries.usageNote: 'To be blunt' prefaces honesty that might sting. Less warm than 'candid', less harsh than 'brusque'. Also literal (a blunt instrument).

entries.definition: A hopeful or positive aspect found within an otherwise difficult situation.
entries.plain: The bright side of a bad situation.
entries.etymology: From the proverb 'every cloud has a silver lining'.
collocations: every cloud has a silver lining
entries.exampleClinical: The silver lining of the long admission was that we finally got his diabetes properly under control.
entries.exampleCasual: The flight was cancelled, but the silver lining was an extra day at the beach.
entries.usageNote: From 'every cloud has a silver lining'. 'The silver lining is...' introduces the redeeming upside of a setback.

entries.term: to err on the side of caution
entries.definition: To choose the safer option when uncertain, even if it may be unnecessary.
entries.plain: To play it safe when you're not sure.
entries.etymology: From 'err' (to make a mistake) — if you must lean, lean toward safety.
collocations: err on the side of caution
we erred on the side of caution
entries.exampleClinical: The scan was probably normal, but we erred on the side of caution and admitted her overnight.
entries.exampleCasual: I erred on the side of caution and packed an umbrella, which of course guaranteed sunshine.
entries.usageNote: 'Err' here is pronounced 'ur' by most speakers. A staple of clinical reasoning where safety outweighs the cost of over-acting.

entries.term: off the top of my head
entries.definition: From memory and without checking, giving an approximate, immediate answer.
entries.plain: Just from memory, without looking it up.
entries.etymology: Idiomatic — an answer that comes straight off the surface of the mind.
collocations: off the top of my head
I can't say off the top of my head
entries.exampleClinical: Off the top of my head the dose is about five milligrams, but check it before you give it.
entries.exampleCasual: Off the top of my head I can name maybe three of the capitals — don't quiz me.
entries.usageNote: Signals an unchecked, approximate answer and quietly hedges responsibility. Very common spoken disclaimer before a guess.

entries.definition: With knowledge or understanding that only became available after the event.
entries.plain: Looking back, now that you know how it turned out.
entries.etymology: From 'hind' (back) + 'sight' — seeing backward.
entries.exampleClinical: In hindsight the early signs were all there, but at the time they looked like an ordinary virus.
entries.exampleCasual: In hindsight, replying to that email at 2 a.m. was not my finest decision.
entries.usageNote: 'In hindsight' and 'in retrospect' are interchangeable. 'Hindsight is 20/20' warns against judging past decisions by later knowledge.

entries.definition: Used to point out that something is much harder to do than it is to suggest.
entries.plain: Simple to say, hard to actually do.
entries.etymology: A proverb attested since the 15th century.
entries.exampleClinical: 'Just reduce your stress' is easier said than done when you're working three jobs.
entries.exampleCasual: Saving money on a student income is easier said than done.
entries.usageNote: A gentle pushback on glib advice. Fixed phrase — don't alter the wording. Acknowledges difficulty without refusing outright.

entries.definition: To decide how to handle a situation as it develops rather than planning in advance.
entries.plain: To improvise as things unfold.
entries.etymology: From music — playing without sheet music, by ear.
entries.exampleClinical: We'll start the antibiotics and play it by ear depending on how she responds overnight.
entries.exampleCasual: I haven't planned the weekend — let's just play it by ear.
entries.usageNote: Musical origin (playing without a score). Means staying flexible and reactive. Informal but common even in professional settings.

entries.definition: Present, appearing, or found everywhere.
entries.plain: Seemingly everywhere at once.
entries.etymology: Latin ubique 'everywhere'.
entries.exampleClinical: This organism is ubiquitous in soil, so growing it from a wound rarely means much on its own.
entries.exampleCasual: Oat-milk lattes have become absolutely ubiquitous in this part of town.
entries.usageNote: Formal but increasingly common. Often slightly ironic ('the ubiquitous selfie'). Stronger than 'common' — implies literally everywhere.

entries.definition: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically rather than by fixed theory.
entries.plain: Practical and realistic rather than idealistic.
entries.etymology: Greek pragmatikos 'relating to fact', from pragma (deed).
entries.exampleClinical: Guidelines aside, you have to be pragmatic about what this particular patient will actually manage at home.
entries.exampleCasual: She took a pragmatic view of the breakup and just focused on splitting the furniture.
entries.usageNote: Strongly positive in professional contexts — values workable reality over theory. Noun: pragmatism. Opposite of 'dogmatic'.

entries.definition: Stated or appearing to be true, but not necessarily so.
entries.plain: The supposed reason, which may not be the real one.
entries.etymology: Latin ostendere 'to show'.
entries.exampleClinical: The ostensible reason for the visit was a cough, but the real worry surfaced only at the end.
entries.exampleCasual: The ostensible purpose of the meeting was planning; the actual purpose was free pizza.
entries.usageNote: The adjective behind 'ostensibly'. Signals a stated-but-suspect reason. Pairs with reason, purpose, aim.

entries.definition: A state of uncertainty or perplexity, especially over a difficult choice.
entries.plain: Being stuck over a hard decision.
entries.etymology: Origin uncertain; perhaps a play on Latin quando (when).
entries.exampleClinical: We were in a quandary: every treatment that would help the heart risked harming the kidneys.
entries.exampleCasual: I'm in a quandary over which job to take — both have a serious catch.
entries.usageNote: Emphasizes mental indecision more than the situation itself (compare 'predicament'). 'In a quandary' is the usual frame.

entries.definition: Very careful to do everything correctly and with moral exactness.
entries.plain: Carefully thorough and ethically careful.
entries.etymology: Latin scrupulus 'small sharp stone, source of unease'.
entries.exampleClinical: Scrupulous hand hygiene is unglamorous and saves more lives than most of what we do.
entries.exampleCasual: He's scrupulous about splitting the bill to the exact cent.
entries.usageNote: Carries a moral edge (correctness, honesty) on top of carefulness. 'Unscrupulous' (without principles) is the common negative.

entries.definition: Not harmful or offensive; harmless, often deceptively so.
entries.plain: Harmless — sometimes more harmless-looking than it really is.
entries.etymology: Latin innocuus 'harmless', from in- (not) + nocere (to harm).
entries.exampleClinical: The mole looked innocuous, but something about the irregular border earned it a biopsy.
entries.exampleCasual: It started with an innocuous question and somehow became a two-hour debate.
entries.usageNote: Often 'seemingly innocuous' — harmless on the surface, not underneath. Shares the 'noc' (harm) root with 'noxious'.

entries.definition: Spreading widely throughout and present in every part of something.
entries.plain: Spread all through something.
entries.etymology: Latin pervadere 'to go through', from per- + vadere (to go).
entries.exampleClinical: There was a pervasive sense of fatigue across the whole team by the end of the run of nights.
entries.exampleCasual: There's a pervasive smell of fresh paint in the new flat that just won't shift.
entries.usageNote: Implies seeping through everything, often subtly and unwelcomely. 'A pervasive sense of' fits moods and atmospheres especially well.

entries.definition: To consider and compare the different factors before making a decision.
entries.plain: To compare the pros and cons.
entries.etymology: From weighing items on a balance.
collocations: weigh up the pros and cons
entries.exampleClinical: You're constantly weighing up the benefit of the scan against the radiation it costs.
entries.exampleCasual: I'm still weighing up whether the gym membership is worth it.
entries.usageNote: 'Weigh up the options/pros and cons/risks'. The balance-scale metaphor for deliberate comparison. Common in decision talk.

entries.definition: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something at the same time.
entries.plain: Pulled in two directions about something.
entries.etymology: Latin ambi- (both) + valere (to be strong) — strong feelings both ways.
entries.exampleClinical: She was ambivalent about the surgery — wanting the cure, dreading the recovery — and that's worth exploring, not overriding.
entries.exampleCasual: I'm pretty ambivalent about the new café; the coffee's great but the music is a war crime.
entries.usageNote: Not the same as 'indifferent' (no feelings); ambivalence is two strong feelings at once. Takes 'about'. Noun: ambivalence.

entries.definition: To gradually accept a difficult or painful reality.
entries.plain: To make peace with something hard.
entries.etymology: From negotiating 'terms' — reaching an agreement, here with reality.
collocations: come to terms with the diagnosis
come to terms with the loss
entries.exampleClinical: He's still coming to terms with the diagnosis, so push the big decisions a little further down the road.
entries.exampleCasual: I'm slowly coming to terms with the fact that I'll never be a morning person.
entries.usageNote: About emotional acceptance of hard truths (loss, diagnosis, failure). Often progressive: 'still coming to terms with'. Central to clinical empathy.

entries.definition: Showing good judgment; sensible and carefully considered.
entries.plain: Wisely and carefully decided.
entries.etymology: Latin judicium 'judgment', from judex (judge).
entries.exampleClinical: The judicious use of fluids — enough but not too much — is half the art of managing sepsis.
entries.exampleCasual: A judicious amount of caffeine helps; a less judicious amount produces this exact text at 3 a.m.
entries.usageNote: 'Judicious use of' is the signature collocation — wise restraint as much as wise action. Adverb: judiciously.

entries.definition: To confirm or support the truth of something with evidence over time.
entries.plain: To prove something right in the end.
entries.etymology: From 'bear' (to carry, support) + 'out' (to completion).
entries.exampleClinical: Her hunch about the rare diagnosis was borne out by the genetic test weeks later.
entries.exampleCasual: If the forecast is borne out, we're in for a soggy weekend.
entries.usageNote: Often passive: 'borne out by the evidence' (note the spelling 'borne'). A more idiomatic alternative to 'confirm' or 'corroborate'.

entries.definition: Without intention; by accident or oversight.
entries.plain: By accident, without meaning to.
entries.etymology: Latin in- (not) + advertere (to turn the mind to).
entries.exampleClinical: The dose was inadvertently doubled when two teams both charted it — a systems error, not a personal one.
entries.exampleCasual: I inadvertently replied-all to the entire department. Twice.
entries.usageNote: Formal alternative to 'by accident'. Adjective: inadvertent. Useful for describing errors without assigning blame.

entries.definition: To accept something unwelcome as unavoidable, making peace with it.
entries.plain: To accept something you can't change.
entries.etymology: From 'reconcile' (to bring back into harmony) + reflexive.
entries.exampleClinical: Over the months he reconciled himself to a slower pace of life than the one he'd planned.
entries.exampleCasual: I've reconciled myself to the fact that my houseplants and I have irreconcilable differences.
entries.usageNote: Reflexive and formal: 'reconcile yourself to'. Close to 'resign oneself to' but slightly less defeatist. Distinct from reconciling two facts.

entries.definition: Clear and definite enough to be perceived or measured; or literally able to be touched.
entries.plain: Real and concrete enough to feel or measure.
entries.etymology: Latin tangere 'to touch'.
entries.exampleClinical: After two weeks there was a tangible improvement — not just numbers, but how he actually felt.
entries.exampleCasual: I want tangible progress on this project, not just another inspiring meeting.
entries.usageNote: Figurative ('tangible benefits') and literal ('tangible object'). Opposite 'intangible'. 'Palpable' is a near-synonym, especially of atmospheres.

entries.definition: To remain valid or applicable across cases or over time.
entries.plain: To stay true in other cases too.
entries.etymology: From 'hold' (to remain valid) + 'true'.
entries.exampleClinical: The rule of thumb holds true for adults, but it breaks down badly in small children.
entries.exampleCasual: Be kind to people on the way up — that old advice still holds true.
entries.usageNote: 'Holds true for [cases]'. A clean academic way to extend or limit a generalization. 'The same holds true' links parallel claims.

entries.definition: To base or found something on a particular fact or assumption.
entries.plain: To base one thing on another.
entries.etymology: Latin praedicare 'to proclaim', from prae- + dicare (to declare).
entries.exampleClinical: The whole plan is predicated on her being able to inject the medication herself at home.
entries.exampleCasual: His optimism was predicated entirely on a weather forecast that turned out to be wrong.
entries.usageNote: Almost always passive: 'predicated on/upon'. Means resting on an assumption or condition. Formal and academic.

entries.definition: To cause gradual harm, damage, or loss over time.
entries.plain: To gradually wear something or someone down.
entries.etymology: From 'toll' — a payment exacted, here exacted by hardship.
entries.exampleClinical: Years of poorly controlled pressure take their toll on the kidneys long before any symptom shows.
entries.exampleCasual: The back-to-back deadlines really took their toll on my sleep.
entries.usageNote: 'Take its toll ON something/someone'. Emphasizes slow, cumulative damage. A vivid alternative to 'damage' or 'wear down'.

entries.definition: Directly relevant to the matter at hand.
entries.plain: Relevant to exactly what's being discussed.
entries.etymology: Latin pertinere 'to relate to', from per- + tenere (to hold).
entries.exampleClinical: In the history, 'pertinent negatives' — the relevant things the patient does NOT have — matter as much as the positives.
entries.exampleCasual: Let's stick to the pertinent details; we don't need his entire life story.
entries.usageNote: 'Pertinent negatives/positives' is core clinical-presentation vocabulary. Takes 'to'. 'Germane' is a more formal synonym.

entries.definition: To perform competently and not be overwhelmed, despite difficulty or strong competition.
entries.plain: To keep up and not fall behind.
entries.etymology: From 'hold' (to maintain) + 'one's own' (position).
entries.exampleClinical: She's frail but holding her own — stable overnight, no new oxygen, eating a little.
entries.exampleCasual: He more than held his own in a debate against people twice his age.
entries.usageNote: Two uses: surviving an illness ('holding her own') and competing well. Possessive matches the subject: 'hold his/her/their own'.
